---
title: "WMATA Line Chart Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the WMATA Line Chart activity, which aggregates daily data to weekly totals and creates a line chart.

## Aggregating dates with `floor_date()`

```
weekly_wmata <- wmata |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarize(
    weekly_total = sum(total),
    days = n()
  ) |>
  filter(days == 7)
```

`floor_date(date, "week")` rounds each date down to the start of its week (the preceding Sunday). All days in the same week get the same value, so you can then `group_by(week)` to aggregate. `sum(total)` adds up daily ridership within each week. `n()` counts how many days fell in that week.

`filter(days == 7)` removes partial weeks (like the first and last weeks in the data, which might only have 3 or 4 days). Including partial weeks would make them look artificially low on the chart.

You can also use `"month"`, `"quarter"`, or `"year"` instead of `"week"` to aggregate at different levels.

## Line chart with trend line

```
weekly_wmata |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = weekly_total)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)
```

`geom_line()` connects the weekly data points with a line. `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` overlays a straight trend line, making it easier to see whether ridership is generally going up or down. `linetype = "dashed"` makes the trend line visually distinct from the data line.

`scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)` formats the y-axis numbers with commas (1,500,000 instead of 1500000). The `scales::comma` part is a formatting function from the `scales` package — you do not need to load the full package when you reference it this way.

## Common mistakes

**Forgetting to filter partial weeks:**

```
# Wrong — includes partial first/last weeks that look artificially low:
weekly_wmata <- wmata |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarize(weekly_total = sum(total))

# Correct — count days per week and keep only full weeks:
weekly_wmata <- wmata |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarize(weekly_total = sum(total), days = n()) |>
  filter(days == 7)
```

A partial week (say, only 3 days) will have a much lower total than a full week. Without filtering, it creates a misleading dip at the start or end of your chart.

**Using `geom_bar()` when you mean `geom_line()`:**

```
# geom_bar() — for categorical x-axis (days of week, categories):
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = total)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity")

# geom_line() — for continuous x-axis (dates, time series):
ggplot(data, aes(x = date, y = total)) + geom_line()
```

Line charts connect points over a continuous sequence (like time). Bar charts compare discrete categories. Using bars for time series data makes the chart harder to read.

**Forgetting `method = "lm"` in `geom_smooth()`:**

```
# Without method, geom_smooth() uses a curvy line (LOESS by default):
geom_smooth()

# With method = "lm", it draws a STRAIGHT trend line:
geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

LOESS (the default) follows the data closely and curves. A linear trend line (`"lm"`) shows the overall direction. Use `"lm"` when you want to show whether something is generally going up or down.
